title: What happens if a service crashes during an update using asynchronous communication, and how do you handle it (ack+retry, idempotency, DLQ, transactional outbox, circuit breaker, saga)?
shortTitle: What happens if a service crashes during an update using asynchronous communication
keyPoints: With manual ack and at-least-once delivery, an unacknowledged message is redelivered after a crash, so no work is lost.
Idempotency is the single most important defense: processing a message twice must produce the same result as once.
A dead-letter queue catches poison messages that always fail, so they do not block good messages.
The transactional outbox guarantees the producer never loses an event by writing it atomically with the business change.
A circuit breaker stops the consumer from flooding a dependency that is already down.
A Saga with compensating transactions handles multi-step workflows that span services.
These mechanisms compose: outbox guarantees publication, ack+retry guarantees delivery, idempotency makes redelivery safe.

s1_definition.oneliner: A crash means the unacknowledged message is redelivered, so you survive it with manual ack plus retry, idempotent processing, a dead-letter queue, a transactional outbox, and a Saga for multi-step work.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Manual acknowledgment** – The consumer acknowledges a message only after the business work has durably committed, never on receipt.
- **Idempotency** – Processing the same message multiple times produces the same result, typically enforced with an inbox table of processed message IDs.
- **Dead-letter queue (DLQ)** – A holding queue for messages that always fail, so poison messages are parked for inspection instead of blocking the partition.
- **Transactional outbox** – The producer writes the event into an outbox table in the same transaction as the business change, eliminating the dual-write problem.
- **Saga** – For multi-step workflows, compensating transactions undo committed steps when a later step fails.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, a back-office clerk takes a transfer slip from the inbox tray and starts working. If the clerk faints halfway, the rule is that the slip stays in the inbox because the clerk only moves it to the done tray after the work is fully finished. When the clerk recovers, the slip gets redone. To make sure Rajesh is not charged twice, each slip has a unique stamp the clerk checks first. Slips that keep causing problems are moved to a special tray for a supervisor.

sections.s6_takeaway:
When a consumer crashes during asynchronous processing, the broker redelivers the unacknowledged message, so no work is lost. But the same message may be delivered more than once, which is the central design challenge. The layered defense starts with manual acknowledgment so messages are only acked after the business change commits, then idempotency so processing twice produces the same result, then a dead-letter queue so poison messages that always fail are parked instead of blocking good ones.

On the producer side, the transactional outbox guarantees events are never lost by writing the event atomically with the business change. A circuit breaker stops the consumer from flooding a dependency that is already down, and for multi-step workflows a Saga runs compensating transactions. These mechanisms compose: the outbox guarantees publication, at-least-once plus manual ack guarantees delivery, idempotency makes redelivery safe, the DLQ contains poison, and the Saga keeps multi-step work consistent.

At National Bank of India, a consumer once credited Priya, crashed before acknowledging, and the redelivered message credited her a second time. Pankaj added an inbox-based idempotency check keyed by message ID. A malformed message with a null account ID failed every retry and starved the partition, so they added a DLQ after three attempts. And a producer that updated the ledger then crashed before publishing left a downstream blind, so they moved to a transactional outbox.

Remember one sentence: a crash means the unacknowledged message is redelivered, so design for safe redelivery with manual ack, idempotent processing, a DLQ for poison, a transactional outbox so events are never lost, and a Saga for multi-step consistency.
